9.t: The Savoy Bearcats, Willie Lynch and Fess Williams
9.s: Discussion of who played the Savoy then: the Savoy Bearcats with drummer Willie Lynch, and a clarinetist who was a great technician.
9.q: Yeah, the Bearcats were there. I'm sure it was the Bearcats. Yeah, I think it was the Bearcats. Because I remember when Fess played there, there was a big opening for him, you know. I think Fess was away at that time.

9.t: Willie Lynch's band at the Savoy and how it was founded
9.s: Holmes recalls Willie Lynch of the Savoy Bearcats forming a band for the Savoy manager, with Holmes on alto, earning more than Chick Webb's band.
9.ch: Willie Lynch, the Blue Rhythm Band and Teddy Hill
9.q: He was out of the Savoy Bearcats band, which was one of the first bands...which was the first band to open the Savoy, you know. He was the drummer in the band. And I think that was Duncan Mayo's band. I think Duncan Mayo was the leader of that band. Well, that was in 1926, that the Savoy opened up…

9.t: Joining Teddy Hill's band at the Savoy
9.s: Teddy Hill hired him after the Blue Rhythm Band; Holmes lists the personnel including Blanchard, Pinkett, Sam Allen and Bill Beason, with Roy Eldridge replacing Pinkett.
9.ch: Willie Lynch, the Blue Rhythm Band and Teddy Hill
9.q: : Teddy Hill was forming a band, or he had a band in the Savoy Ballroom... No, he was getting ready to go in the Savoy Ballroom. And he heard I had come' out of the Blue Rhythm Band. So he asked me if I wanted a job, and I said, "Sure." So I worked at the Savoy on numerous occasions.

9.t: First night at the Savoy Ballroom, thrown off the floor
9.s: Holmes and Carney arrive in March 1927, are awed by the Savoy, and bouncers push them off the dance floor when they try to greet Hodges.
9.q: : '27. 1927. I'll never forget it. I think it was March the twelfth, but I wouldn't bet on it because they changed the dates around. I know at the Savoy Ballroom, the next night after we got here, they had an anniversary dance at the Savoy Ballroom the next night. The Savoy had only been open one…

9.t: Lou Henry's offer to play the Savoy and Carney's advice
9.s: Tired of Brooklyn, he took Carney's advice that the Savoy would put him on view and accepted Lou Henry's three-month job.
9.q: : So we stayed there, they stayed there until around December. And I was talking to Harry Carney -- he was still rooming with me, you know. Of course, I'm down here at the beach and he...

9.t: Lou Henry's band personnel and the thrill of the Savoy
9.s: He names those he remembers in Lou Henry's band and recalls how glamorous working at the Savoy was.
9.q: The reed section... I know who the reed section was. It was Bob Holmes, and the tenor player's name was Tramp -- he's dead now...Trent. Not Alfonso Trent. He was a tenor player. Anyway, let me see. There was Anderson... I don't remember who else was in the trumpets.

9.t: The Savoy beat and Russell's band winning band battles
9.s: Only young people could dance to swing; the right beat won applause and Russell's band, in and out of the Savoy like a house band, beat all rivals.
9.ch: Russell's band, records and Armstrong in the studio
9.q: Oh yeah. Only young people could do it. The old ones do it and break their neck. All the young ones couldn't do it -- because I didn't want to do it. Yeah, it was strictly young people's music. That swinging music, that's strictly for young folks. At the Savoy you had that bright beat. You didn't…

9.t: Chick Webb's enlarged band on ten New England dates
9.s: Webb enlarged to ten pieces for a New England tour with Hodges, Williams and the Savoy band, but the band rehearsed constantly and found little work.
9.q: So I think when Lou Henry's contract ran out... He was there three months. I think that's when... Well, that's when I went to Chick Webb. I think I went with Chick then. Because Chick wasn't doing anything, and he was getting ready to go to Boston. -- he had ten dates up in New England. So he was…

9.t: Cootie Williams and Alonzo Ross's band join Chick Webb
9.s: Webb enlarged to ten pieces by adding Holmes and Cootie Williams, who came from Alonzo Ross's broken-up Florida band that included Cass Carr.
9.ch: Cass Carr, Crawley, Burnet and Cootie Williams
9.q: Well, I was telling you about the time I went with Chick's band, Chick Webb. He had an eight-piece band at the Savoy Ballroom, and he was enlarging the band to ten pieces. And he added myself and Cootie Williams on trumpet to the band, which enlarged it to ten pieces.

70.t: The Savoy Ballroom's early years: Fess Williams and Chick Webb
70.s: Fess Williams opened the Savoy in 1926; Chick Webb's eight-piece band followed with Hodges, Cootie Williams and Truehart.
70.ch: Harlem, Redman's band and the Savoy
70.q: And then Chick -- Chick Webb was in there, too. Chick Webb had an eight-piece band. He had two saxophones in there. He had Johnny Hodges on alto and Elmer Williams on tenor, and he had Cootie Williams on trumpet. I don't know who the bass player was.

70.t: The Savoy house bands, Basie, and the Savoy Sultans
70.s: Chick Webb was the main Savoy band, followed by Basie and the Alabama State Collegians; the Savoy Sultans, musically rough, outswung everyone for dancers.
70.ch: Harlem, Redman's band and the Savoy
70.q: Then, going back to the Savoy Ballroom later on, Chick was always the main band there and he enlarged his band, you know, and he always was the house band there. Then later Basie came and the Alabama State Collegians.

70.t: Teddy Hill's band at the Savoy
70.s: Teddy Hill's band, second only to Webb's, had Dillard, Collins, Eldridge, Dickie Wells, Procope, Chu Berry and a high-playing brass section.
70.ch: Harlem, Redman's band and the Savoy
70.q: Yeah, two altos. -- and Choo Berry was the tenor. And Sam Allen was the pianist and old man Fulbright -- I forget his first name -- he was the bass player.

70.t: Break for a bite and turning to the Savoy Ballroom
70.s: Hinton notes they are having a bite, and moves to the Savoy Ballroom, with Jackson asking to start before he came to New York.
70.ch: Harlem, Redman's band and the Savoy
70.q: Could I go before I came to New York about the Savoy Ballroom because --

70.t: Russell Procope and Edgar Sampson in Henderson's band
70.s: Jackson met Procope and violinist and composer Edgar Sampson in Henderson's band in 1932; Sampson wrote Stompin' at the Savoy and Blue Lou.
70.ch: Harlem, Redman's band and the Savoy
70.q: He was playing with Fletcher. He was playing with Fletcher then. And a great violinist, too, was playing with Fletcher then, Edgar Sampson. He was in Fletcher's band when I first came to New York.

70.t: Erskine Hawkins, the Bama State Collegians and Dud Bascomb's Tuxedo Junction solo
70.s: The Collegians came to the Savoy by school bus, Moe Gale billed Hawkins as the Twentieth Century Gabriel, but Dud Bascomb's solo made Tuxedo Junction.
70.ch: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
70.q: Erskine Hawkins was a high note trumpet player. He was one of these trumpet players that he was a very quiet guy and until you heard him play you wouldn't even know what he was going to say or what he was going to do until he got in front of the bandstand. He was a very quiet bandleader, too. The…

70.t: Chick Webb's band as a source of musicians
70.s: Webb's eight-piece band gave Hodges and Cootie Williams to Duke and once had Jimmy Harrison.
70.ch: Harlem, Redman's band and the Savoy
70.q: Do you know Chick Webb had a lot of great musicians in his band. A lot of great musicians came out of his band to go to other bands, you know. At one time Jimmy Harrison played with Chick Webb before he went to Fletcher. Chick Webb only had eight pieces. And Johnny Hodges played with Chick Webb.…

113.t: Savoy stays, Gale bookings and Don Redman billing
113.s: The band alternated weeks in and out of the Savoy, was booked by Gale in theatres and nearby territory, and played Christmas dates billed as Redman's.
113.ch: Decca records, the Savoy and Moe Gale
113.q: We'd go in there on two weeks and out two, I think on that trip, we stayed there three weeks. I think we were there three weeks that trip and was out for a week, come back in for two and were out for two weeks and come back in for two. That's the way they used to do it. They had their bands.

113.s: McShann held back for three sets, then the band went into its books and out-played Lucky Millinder's, who afterwards fired three men.
113.ch: Decca records, the Savoy and Moe Gale
113.q: And so we went in with this particular night, whatever night it was, we opened up with Lucky's band and so I told the cats, I said, look, man, they tell me Lucky is one of the favorites around here. What I think we ought to do we'll just play it kind of cool. We'll play some stocks for about the…

113.t: Out-swinging Lucky Millinder's band in New York
113.s: Sharing the bandstand with Millinder's band, McShann's group tightened up, got into its books and won the crowd with swing.
113.ch: The New York band and Charlie Parker
113.q: Oh, yes. See — see at that time Lucky had quite a band and Lucky seemed to be, he was about the most feared group around there. And so they had the number one and number two bandstand and so it was, what they do is I think they start you out on number two and then after you figure you’re pretty…

113.t: Ben Webster tells 52nd Street to go uptown to the Savoy
113.s: Ben Webster told saxophonists on 52nd Street to go to the Savoy to learn from the young Kansas City band, and funnily described them sneaking in.
113.ch: Decca records, the Savoy and Moe Gale
113.q: Oh, yes, the word got around, but it takes Benny Webster to tell it though. Benny Webster because he came up, had been catching the group and he went downtown on 52nd Street and says, now, all you guys that call yourselves saxophone players, he says, you better go uptown to the Savoy Ballroom and…

113.t: Arriving at the Savoy in 1941 with the Sultans
113.s: They opened at the Savoy Ballroom in 1941, after Chick Webb's death, playing a private party and then alongside the Sultans.
113.ch: Decca records, the Savoy and Moe Gale
113.q: they just ate it up so then we went on to New York, and Tim Gail came in and caught us at Gary and he sat and we talked and he says well, we're going to bring you guys on into New York at the Savoy Ballroom and going to try to do some business together and do somethings and we talked okay. And so…

0.t: Savoy house bands, Fess Williams and Edgar Sampson
0.s: They split the Savoy with Chick Webb in 1927-28, moved to the Colonnades in 1929; Sampson later arranged for Chick, Duke and Fletcher.
0.ch: Arthur Gibbs, Savoy Ballroom and recording sessions
0.q: No, let me see. The dance part, the thing Chick had [John] Trueheart (unintelligible) on guitar, and we had Paul Burnet on banjo, and then the same, trumpet, trombone, two instrumentation saxophone, bass, piano and drums, same as (unintelligible).

0.t: Andrade's band outplays Cab Calloway at the Savoy
0.s: Andrade's band was booked at the Savoy; one night they were so good Cab's band could not get back on the stand.
0.ch: Vernon Andrade's band and Harlem life
0.q: Yeah, we played the theaters, and we had entertainment in the Saville. Louie would sing, and George Washington would sing, and we had the group would sing. And we stayed with -- stationed there on the -- and then we went up to the Savoy too.

0.t: Arthur Gibbs's band at the Savoy and Colonnades: personnel
0.s: Caldwell played tenor in Arthur Gibbs's ten-piece band, with Billy Taylor, Sammy Hodges and Edgar Sampson; Gibbs wrote Running Wild.
0.ch: Arthur Gibbs, Savoy Ballroom and recording sessions
0.q: Savoy Ballroom. Then we left the Savoy Ballroom and went down to the -- to the big ballroom on Broadway. It's not there now. They tore it -- they closed it up about seven --

0.t: Arrangers and Chick Webb's band as the other Savoy house band
0.s: Sammy Hodges and others arranged; Chick Webb's band on the other bandstand included Elmer Williams, Johnny Hodges and Cuffe.
0.ch: Arthur Gibbs, Savoy Ballroom and recording sessions
0.q: like Sammy Hodges, the drummer, arrangements like different ones would make arrangements, for the There was nine of us because Chick Webb's band was on band. (Unintelligible) in the other bandstand.

0.t: Covering for Hawkins in Fletcher's band while with Arthur Gibbs
0.s: Hawk would leave when Fletcher came in; Caldwell played sets with Gibbs and Fletcher at the Savoy and Roseland and got two pays.
0.ch: Small's Paradise, Fletcher Henderson and Horace
0.q: Worked with Fletcher for -- and Hawk would always take off. But every time Fletcher would come in, Hawk would take off. He didn't care. So Hawk would call me when he worked at the club.

124.t: Savoy Ballroom contest against Fess Williams
124.s: Invited to the Savoy to play against Fess Williams, the band surprised the audience, who had not known it was Black; the bassist played a pedal-type bass.
124.ch: Philadelphia and the McRae Brothers Band, 1908-1929
124.q: brass. And people thought that this was a band from out West, you know. And when we went to the Savoy, we played -- They invited us to the Savoy one Sunday to paly against Fess William. And everybody was astonished to find out that this band was a colored band and had been in town for about a month…

124.t: Back at the Savoy: broadcasts and college dates
124.s: After the road trip the band broadcast from the Savoy and played holiday dates at Yale and Harvard.
124.ch: With Chick Webb and Ella Fitzgerald, 1936-39
124.q: went back in the Savoy. We used to go out and do -- on holidays, we do the colleges, like Yale, Harvard, you know -- and things like that.

124.t: Boston engagement at La Vodges with Artie Shaw's band
124.s: Chick's band broke records at a Boston eatery while Artie Shaw's band played nearby, where McRae started writing for Shaw.
124.ch: With Chick Webb and Ella Fitzgerald, 1936-39
124.q: That was like when Artie Shaw was there (and I (inaudible)) started writing with Artie. I think it was in '37 or '38. Working for (inaudible) both bands. Artie went to Boston and Chick Webb was in Boston, (inaudible) LaVodges.

124.t: Webb's battles with Goodman, Casa Loma and Duke
124.s: McRae thinks the Goodman battle was overblown; Webb outplayed Casa Loma with "Hold That Tiger" and respected Duke's band.
124.ch: Life on the road and in the Webb band's book
124.q: The one we had with Duke Ellington and Chick Webb at the Savoy on Sunday night, I think this was the most outstanding battle of music, much better than the Benny Goodman battle.

124.t: Replacing Elmer Williams in Chick Webb's saxes
124.s: Elmer Williams would not travel, and Chick had promised McRae the job; the band was house band at the Savoy.
124.ch: With Chick Webb and Ella Fitzgerald, 1936-39
124.q: Elmer. Elmer didn't want to go on the road, because he always told me -- he say, "You are my next tenor player." He always kept me in mind.

149.t: Sharing audiences with Chick Webb and Jimmie Lunceford
149.s: At the Savoy his band and Webb's alternated; with Lunceford he shared a 10,000-person Philadelphia show.
149.q: Oh, yes. We did, especially when we were together at the Savoy cause when Chick would go on, he'd go and play 45 minutes. And then, when he'd take his break, I was on for 45 minutes. So, that's the same audience. They were standing right in front of the band all the same time. And the people, they…

149.t: The Savoy: Goodman-Webb battle and the swinging floor
149.s: He describes the crowded block and the floor bouncing at the Goodman-Webb battle.
149.ch: Savoy days, the Concord and business
149.q: I remember the time that Chick Webb and Benny Goodman, they was at that time — is that it? [Second tape records]

149.t: Tiny Bradshaw, Lucky Millinder and manager Charlie Buchanan
149.s: He recalls other Savoy bandleaders and the manager who booked the bands.
149.ch: Savoy days, the Concord and business
149.q: Tiny Bradshaw. He was up the Savoy quite a few times. This was before Chick Webb and Benny Goodman had, they started having those, you know, good Swing sessions up there.

149.t: Staying in New York: Savoy Ballroom, Moe Gale and Chick Webb
149.s: He played Roseland and the Savoy from 1935, where Moe Gale became his manager and he became house band after Chick Webb.
149.ch: Forming the band in New York
149.q: The Savoy was owned by the Gales, Moe Gale. I went up there to play a week, and then he turned out to be my personal manager. That's the reason I stayed in the Savoy so many years. When I got tired of travelling on the road, I'd go and I'd stay like 6 months, 7 months.

428.t: Bands opposite Chick Webb at the Savoy and Jesse Owens's band
428.s: Hall lists bands that played opposite his group at the Savoy and tells how a band was promoted for Jesse Owens and fell apart.
428.ch: New York arrival, Billy Hicks and the Black Cat
428.q: Whoever came in there. Tommy Dorsey, Bunny Berigan, Erskine Hawkins, Teddy Hill, even -- what's the champion runner from Munich, Jesse Owens had a band.

428.t: Bands opposite Chick Webb and Jesse Owens's band (second pass)
428.s: Repeat of the bands at the Savoy and the failed Jesse Owens band.
428.ch: New York 1936-39 (second pass of the transcript)
428.q: Whoever came in there. Tommy Dorsey, Buddy Barrigan, Erskine Hawkins, Teddy Hill, even what's the champion runner for Munich, Hitler --

428.t: Billy Hicks and his Sizzling Six at the Savoy
428.s: Hall names the sidemen, says it was an arranged band playing popular songs, and mentions the pianists of the time.
428.ch: New York arrival, Billy Hicks and the Black Cat
428.q: I started it at the Savoy Ballroom. Bill Hicks got the gig at the Savoy Ballroom, opposite Chick Webb and we stayed a year and a half.

428.t: Billy Hicks and his Sizzling Six (second pass)
428.s: Repeat account of the Savoy engagement, the sidemen and the repertoire, with the pianists of the day.
428.ch: New York 1936-39 (second pass of the transcript)
428.q: Paying me back. And, I started at the Savoy Ballroom, Billy Hicks got the gig at the Savoy Ballroom opposite Chick Webb. And we stayed a year and a half.

381.t: Six years with Lucky, constant fights, and credit as David Francis
381.s: He stayed six years though he and Lucky argued weekly, and early records list him as David Francis.
381.q: Yeah, that was before they started calling me Panama. Few people were calling me Panama then, I was still David Francis.

381.t: Auditioning for Lucky Millinder at the Savoy
381.s: Trevor Bacon recruits him; he outplays Shadow Wilson at a Savoy audition and wins the job.
381.q: And after I left there, Trevor Bacon was at the show; he caught the show, and he came backstage, and he wanted to know how long was I going to be staying with Roy Eldridge, and I asked him why, and he said that Lucky was looking for a drummer.

381.t: Leading his own band at the Savoy in 1946, then Willie Bryant
381.s: Mr. Buchanan promised a house-band slot, but Tab Smith's group got it and he lost money.
381.q: I went in to the Savoy -- Mr. Buchanan had promised me to bring a band into the Savoy, and if the dancers liked the band, he would use me as the house band because the Savoy Sultans had broken up, and they were looking for a small band to take their place.

18.t: Harlem in the mid-1930s: Lafayette Theatre and Chick Webb at the Savoy
18.s: Mrs. H describes Sundays at the Lafayette Theatre and the Savoy where he played with Chick Webb.
18.ch: Family, Margaret's story and Eutris's memories
18.q: I'll let him go through it and get all the dates. It's all back there somewhere, the date he went with Louis Armstrong, Fletcher Henderson. But I do know he came to New York. Chick Webb heard him, you know, and he went to play with Chick Webb, played the Savoy. I hadn't seen him for years and Edgar…

18.t: White bands at the Savoy Ballroom
18.s: White bands played the Savoy in the early 1930s and about ten percent of the dancers were white.
18.ch: Union, publishers, race and Harlem nightlife
18.q: Playing for anybody. Sure, they'd dance together, just like you walk and talk in the street today.

18.t: Playing across from Whiteman at Roseland; white bands with black players
18.s: They played opposite Whiteman at Roseland; Dorsey featured Charlie Shavers.
18.ch: Union, publishers, race and Harlem nightlife
18.q: Across from the Roseland when it first opened. I told you that the other night. The Beer Barrel Polka came out. Just in front of the Roseland, just opposite, one on one side and one on the other. And they had two bands.

78.t: Alvin Burroughs and the battle with Chick Webb at the Chicago Savoy
78.s: Drummer Alvin 'Mouse' Burroughs came from Earl Hines' band; in a battle of bands before 5,000 people against Chick Webb and Ella Fitzgerald, Horace says his band won.
78.ch: Starting out in New York and Chicago
78.q: Getting the thing over to -- and here's another guy in my band that I had. Unfortunately, he died young. His name was Alvin Burroughs. We called him Mouse. Tom, he was one of the greatest drummers. In fact, I

78.t: Cecil Scott's Syncopaters: Frankie Newton, Don Frye and Savoy showmanship
78.s: Horace met Dickie Wells in Cecil Scott's Springfield band, which battled his Collegians in Ohio; trumpeter Frankie Newton replaced Bill Coleman and the band later stood next to Chick Webb at the Savoy.
78.ch: Portraits from Hemphill to Getz, and the bebop question
78.q: Well, we became friends, and, of course, Don Frye, the pianist in that band, and I are very good friends. Don could always play, and I liked Don's style -- swinging, you know? It seems like -- let's see -- did I miss anybody else in that band? No, I think that's about it. Well, they had a couple of…

78.t: Taking the band to New York: Savoy, Dunbar Palace, Chick Webb
78.s: After graduating Horace was offered New York work near Fletcher and played the Savoy Ballroom next to Chick Webb and the Dunbar Palace. Banjoist Talcott Reeves and the McCord brothers came with him.
78.ch: Starting out in New York and Chicago
78.q: Yes. I had been offered a job in New York to link up with my brother, because there were a couple of clubs there during the Summer that I used to frequent, you know. The Savoy Ballroom, and a place called the Dunbar Palace, (inaudible), and when I graduated, I -- these are some of the jobs that I…

291.t: More of the Savoy band: Kid Ory and Gray
291.s: Barnes adds Kid Ory on trombone and a trumpeter named Gray to the New York Savoy lineup.
291.q: I mean I think it's really hard for now. Well I've had quite a bit of experience in music. I've played with so many of the great musicians. I've played with Johnny Sincere and Kid Ory. I forgot to tell you about the trombone player.

291.t: King Oliver's band at the Savoy Ballroom lineup
291.s: He lists the Oliver band members at the Savoy in New York, with a loop at the end of the trumpet name.
291.q: Well I'll give you a few of them. You see on piano we had Louis Russell on piano, and banjo, Willie Foster, that's Pop Foster's brother, on banjo. On drums we had Paul Barbaran on drums. And on bass we had a bass player called Buford. Now on trumpet we had King Oliver, Red Island, so far back I…

440.t: Chick Webb: promoting him and the Goodman battle of swing
440.s: Hired to make a hit with Chick Webb, she portrays him and stages the battle of swing with Goodman at the Savoy.
440.q: Well anyway, so that office hired me to make a hit with Chick. And Chick, who’d had a wonderful band all those years, and with like Cootie and Johnny, lived in an apartment with Chick, they were all hungry. And they’d had offers but they wouldn’t leave Chick. Johnny was supposed to be Chick’s…

440.t: Logistics and audience of the Savoy battles of the bands
440.s: How bands played side by side, the audience and social balls at the Savoy.
440.q: Well the two bands were side by side you see. And it was a huge floor and it was a mass of human beings. And as I said, the police, the mounted police outside, trying to keep order because it was tremendous. But Chick did own that audience. The minute he’d go boom boom, everybody would scream…

86.t: Battles with other bands; the Savoy and the Swing era
86.s: He recalls battling Lionel Hampton at the Savoy and the Savoy Sultans.
86.ch: Leading the Basie band: music, rivals and recordings
86.q: I can’t say that we did. We did with the Lionel Hampton band. He always wanted to choose Basie because he said his band was better than Basie’s band, we could swing better and everything. So, we just had it out at the Savoy one night. And he never did do that anymore. But you were well entertained…

86.t: Lunceford's band and battles of the bands
86.s: Dance says Basie names Lunceford as another swinging band; Edison recalls battles of the bands and the Savoy.
86.q: Yeah. But you know, they used to have a battle of the bands quite often, you know. And I remember once we had done so many one-nighters and Jimmy Lunceford, you know, he had such a disciplined band. They were all -- he was in the Cotton Club, you know. We never did have a chance to play in the…

65.t: Arrival in New York and the Savoy
65.s: He stayed with his sister Estela and went nightly to the Savoy to hear Chick Webb, where Mario was rehearsing the band.
65.ch: Arriving in New York and founding the Afro-Cubans
65.q: Yes, and I used to go practically every day, every night, to the Savoy because Chick Webb was there building the - - over the radio - the band with Ella Fitzgerald.

65.t: Playing the Apollo and Savoy Ballroom for black audiences
65.s: They played the Savoy twenty-five or thirty times; 95 percent of the audience was black, and danced the Afro-Cuban rhythm well.
65.ch: Chano Pozo, Town Hall and Charlie Parker
65.q: Oh, yes. We played about - in two or three years, we played about twenty-five or thirty times. Two weeks, three weeks, four weeks.

74.t: Chicago vacation, the Savoy and choosing Cleveland over the Arcadia
74.s: They play the Savoy; Meyer Davis wants them at the Arcadia, but Trent takes the Cleveland Plantation job so New York bands cannot raid the men.
74.ch: Trent's band: Texas, St. Louis and the road east
74.q: We came in to play at the Savoy. That's when Meyer Davis wanted to put us in the Arcadia. The Arcadia was the number two ballroom in New York at that time. Of course, Roseland was the number one ballroom and, but in those days Roseland and the Arcadia were real jobs.

74.t: Chicago vacation, the Savoy and the Arcadia offer (second version)
74.s: No Chicago or Detroit jobs; they play the Savoy; Meyer Davis wanted them at the Arcadia but Trent chose Cleveland.
74.ch: Trent's band: Texas, St. Louis and the road east
74.q: Meyer Davis wanted to put us in the Arcadia, but the Arcadia was the number two ballroom in New York at that time. Roseland was the number one ballroom but in those days Roseland and the Arcadia were real jobs. We had the opportunity of going and staying in New York and playing the Arcadia or going…

115.s: In New York the band swung 'Cherokee' on the air at the Savoy and kept it going for the whole half hour.
115.q: And we were in the Savoy Ballroom, and we did "Cherokee," and it was up there fast. (singing).

115.t: Arriving late for the first Savoy night: 'Western Dogs'
115.s: The band's cars broke down, they arrived hours late, and Buchanan made them play all night, outswinging Lucky Millinder and being called Western Dogs.
115.q: When we came to New York, we were late getting there. We were supposed to have been there at 5:00 that evening, to open up.

75.t: Edgar Sampson, "Stomping at the Savoy" and the Empire Ballroom
75.s: Ramirez says the tune was worked out at a Saturday rehearsal, became "Misty Morning," and recalls the Empire Ballroom bands including Chick Webb and Fletcher Henderson.
75.ch: Early 1930s: Bessie Smith, Rex Stewart and the Harlem scene
75.q: : No, he didn't write... How it happened. One Saturday afternoon, during rehearsal, there was a number, a seasonal number -- I don't remember the name of it. We were taking the last chorus to play for David(?) (?). And we sat there, and I got on the piano, and he did...[SINGS FIRST FEW BARS OF…

75.t: Subbing for Tommy Fulford with Chick Webb
75.s: Ramirez played with Chick Webb occasionally when pianist Tommy Fulford, a schoolmate, was sick.
75.q: I don't remember. I think it was Cooper; it could have been Cooper. High school. Not in the early grade schools, you know.

103.t: The battle against Chick Webb at the Savoy and the Carnegie Hall night
103.s: Jones recalls the January 1937 battle of music with Chick Webb, Ella and Billie, the same night as Goodman's Carnegie Hall concert, and Ellington at the Criterion.
103.q: In 1937, January 1937. Yes I have tapes and I have pictures because Chick had Ella, we had Billie. And everybody - the dancers - everybody was looking.....

103.t: Meeting Chick Webb in 1936 and learning his secrets
103.s: Jones recalls the summer of 1936, the Roseland opening, and Webb sharing tuning secrets and encouraging him.
103.q: and then when I came into New York with Basie's band I met him in 1936 - it was the summer of 1936 and I was playing with Victor-Pillars. I left St. Louis and went back to rejoin Basie's band and when I got there, there was no band and no job. I had no thought of coming to New York, but fortunately…

98.t: Tiny Parham's big band at the Savoy
98.s: Saunders worked with Tiny Parham in the mid-1930s; Parham was mostly an arranger who wrote for shows and played a gig band two nights a week.
98.ch: Pianists, Basie, Lil Armstrong and closing
98.q: Yeah, right, he -- I didn't know -- I don't know too much about his history. I worked with him in the Savoy Ballroom. We played the Savoy Ballroom, and then the Savoy Ballroom was on the decline. And then I left out of there and then I went to the Club Delisa. But Tiny --

98.t: Jobbing with Tiny Parham at the Savoy and the naming of Swing
98.s: Weekend work with Tiny Parham's big band at the Savoy Ballroom; the Cobb combo played jazz just as Benny Goodman's Congress Hotel run gave the style the name Swing.
98.q: Yeah, then I went on to gigging, jobbing, you know. That's when I worked with Tiny Parham, yeah, and he had a band in the Savoy Ballroom, and see, every night had gone, we worked Saturdays and Sundays and different nights in the Savoy Ballroom there.

253.t: Moving to New York: Ross, Charlie Skeet and Claude Hopkins
253.s: Hall goes to New York with Ross's band, plays a dancing school, then Charlie Skeet and Claude Hopkins at Roseland and the Savoy.
253.q: Well, different bands, I worked with quite a few different bands. I worked with, let's see, can I get them in rotation? When you first got there, I was thinking about you. When I first got there, well, I went there with Ross's band. We only stayed on the job about two weeks. Then I went into a…

432.t: Winning the 1937 citywide swing contest at St. Monica's
432.s: He describes the lineup that won the contest against Joe Robichaux, Professor Victor and Henry Harden before 10,000 people.
432.q: Well he played saxophone too. But he left here and he went back with, was it Alvin Walters, he went back with, I can't think of them bands, went back to Oklahoma. See they're all from Oklahoma. And they had Porter, trumpet player, Bucket, and all that bunch, they was, and Killdeed they called him,…

188.t: Joining King Oliver and the Savoy in New York
188.s: Having mastered banjo, he left the boat, joined King Oliver's band in St. Louis and went to New York, with a double engagement at the Savoy alongside Chick Webb.
188.q: Well, I knew music already. You already knew it. Oh, yes. When I started my banjo, well, I made good on banjo. I started banjo playing. You know, rated. I left the boat. And I came down here. Oliver sent for me. And I left here from New Orleans and went to St. Louis. It was the King Oliver Band…

47.t: Frank Trumbauer, horseback riding and bands at the Cinderella
47.s: Moore and friends rode horses with Trumbauer in New Jersey; the Wolverines outlasted several bands at the Cinderella, with Fletcher Henderson nearby.
47.q: We were real good friends. George Johnson and Frank and Bob and I, and Bob Gillette and I used to go over to East Orange, and about every Wednesday or Thursday, I forgot, in the afternoon, and go horseback riding. Frank always had an Indian pinto horse in his big hat. Of course he was on…

467.t: Battling Basie at the Savoy Ballroom
467.s: Hampton says his band ran Basie out at the Savoy and describes the showmanship of his young band.
467.q: Yeah, we played against Basie at the Savoy Ballroom in New York. And I don’t want to be stuck up, in no kind of way, but we ran Basie out of the hole that night.

423.t: Lucky Millinder at the Savoy Ballroom
423.s: Ed followed Art Blakey in Lucky Millinder's band at the Savoy, where Lucky warned that if the dancers stopped he was dead; the band played swing and rhythm and blues.
423.q: Well I don’t know, that’s a very good observation, I haven’t really given it very much thought, but I think it’s a good observation for the reason that you’re mentioning, and that is the music of prior years that was still associated with dancing had to have a good feeling to make the dancers feel…

108.t: Playing the Savoy Ballroom and the Savoy Sultans
108.s: Wilder played the Savoy with Millinder, Lunceford, Hawkins and Rushing, describing the dancing crowd, the springy floor, and the Sultans' tempos.
108.q: The Savoy Ballroom, oh yeah, I played the Savoy Ballroom with Lucky Millinder, I played in there with Jimmy Lunceford’s band, I subbed in there a few times with Erskine Hawkins band, Jimmy Rushing had a band, I played with them a few times, I played a lot at the Savoy Ballroom. That was quite a…

1.t: Armstrong's absence and King Oliver's battle with Chick Webb
1.s: Armstrong had gone to Europe after Hot Chocolates, and Barker tells how Chick Webb beat King Oliver at the Savoy with Lindy-hop tempos.
1.q: Armstrong was in Chicago and he was making one-night stands, and he come . . . he had been . . . when I got there, he had been to New York in Hot Chocolates. It was a Broadway show which was a hit. Fats Waller and Andy Razaf wrote the music. Ain’t Misbehavin’, What did I do to be so black and blue,…

85.t: The Savoy Ballroom in 1928: the hall, the Savoy Sultans and the dancing crowd
85.s: Carter describes the Savoy's two bandstands, hostesses, the opposing bands, the book of the Savoy Playboys and the audiences.
85.q: Well, it was a great place to play in and nice, spacious bandstands, of which there were two. Lovely hostesses. Gee, did they . . . it wasn’t ten cents a dance. I don’t know how they operated financially for the hostesses, whether they paid them or what. Because, you know, we could play a pretty…

527.t: A week at the Savoy Ballroom with Lucky Millinder
527.s: Busy recording but no big-band work, then a week at the historic Savoy; Millinder just stomped off tunes and paid fairly.
527.q: Yeah, that was fantastic. I made these records with these guys, and other people would call me up to make records with them also. So, looking back on it, I was busy. I was busy enough and learning all the time. I didn’t do any big band gigs. I didn’t get any

107.t: The Pittsburgh Courier poll win and the Savoy and Carnegie Hall trip
107.s: The Collegians won the first black college dance-band poll partly by stuffing the ballot box, then played the Savoy and a short Carnegie Hall spot.
107.q: Anyway. the Collegians -- now there was a black college dance-band community. The Pittsburgh Courier, the black weekly newspaper, established a Negro college dance-band poll in 1947. The winner of this poll got a trip to New York, a performance at Carnegie Hall on an all-star program, and a…

328.t: The Apollo and the Savoy Ballroom with Bill Doggett's trio
328.s: The family band played a week at the Apollo then opposite Bill Doggett at the Savoy, where they learned about swing.
328.q: It was probably something that wasn’t released, but then, years later, when we played the Savoy Ballroom, we played opposite Bill Doggett’s trio. That’s where we really learned what swing was about.

224.t: Sabby Lewis's band and Osie Johnson replacing him
224.s: Haynes subbed for Joe Booker with Sabby Lewis until Osie Johnson walked in, a fast reader whom the band said did not swing.
224.ch: Early bands and Luis Russell's Harlem
224.q: Sabby Lewis had a – he was the most popular one around Boston then, as a bandleader, because he played – one of his big breaks came when he played one of those big radio shows during the early ’40s, which may have been ’42 or ’41. I don’t remember exactly. It was the Bandwagon – something…

426.s: Ozzie Cadena produced Savoy sessions with a jazz touch, such as Lee Morgan and Hank Mobley dates.
426.q: I think that was produced by Ozzie Cadena. He worked for Savoy during the years that I did. He has much the same attitude as Prestige, rather than Blue Note, even though he worked for Blue Note too. Ozzie knew the music, he knew the way the guys wanted to sound, he got them here on time, and he was…

109.t: Teddy Hill at the 1939 World's Fair and Savoy Pavilion
109.s: About a year and a half with the band, including the 1939 World's Fair, doing 16 appearances a day featuring Lindy Hoppers.
109.q: Oh, let's see. We played the World's Fair with the band, too, in '39. So I was with the band about a year and a half. We did the whole 1939 World's Fair.

80.t: Henderson versus Chick Webb at the Savoy and brother Horace's stolen charts
80.s: At the Savoy Henderson's band finally beat Chick Webb, who usually won because Horace Henderson sold his brother's arrangements to Webb; Autrey loved playing Fletcher's logical, comfortable writing.
80.ch: New York, Henderson and Charlie Johnson
80.q: Yeah. Yeah, after doing this thing we had a -- I think it was a New Year's Eve thing. We did it with Fletcher, and the band went pretty good, and where I was lucky and happy afterwards for doing this recording, and I didn't have the music, and I memorized it, and everything went well.

377.t: Playing opposite Chick Webb and Ella Fitzgerald at the Savoy
377.s: Basie says it was no battle, but exciting to play opposite the First Lady of Swing and Chick Webb's wild band.
377.ch: Billie Holiday with the band (1971 session)
377.q: Well, then, they must have came in for one night or something like that. I don't know which one -- one of the two (inaudible).

17.t: The Rhythm Club, Small's breakfast dances and band battles
17.s: The Band Box/Rhythm Club as the musicians' hangout, jam sessions, Sunday breakfast dances at Small's, and battles at Rockland Palace and the Savoy.
17.q: Oh yeah. All bands. I'll tell you what happened at that club. At the time, Fletcher Henderson was working at the Roseland. Duke was at the Cotton Club I think. I just forget where the Dorseys were playing and Paul Whitman and all the white bands, they were all downtown. But, when everybody would…

66.t: Being called in at the Savoy against Chick Webb, but not hired
66.s: At the Savoy in New York the band called her in to break up Chick Webb's cutting contest, yet she was not made a regular member, partly because of the pianist Jack and because a woman was unusual.
66.ch: Memphis, Oklahoma, the Kirk band and Kansas City
66.q: Well, we scuffled. Let's see, we went to the Savoy in New York. By this time we were playing "Froggy Bottom" and things like that. They called me in to sing because Chick Webb was really blasting town with all bands and they were getting rid of all bands that came in there. I guess you heard about…

67.t: Benny Carter's band at the Savoy and the 1941 record
67.s: Carter's refined band was too polished for jitterbug dancers, who preferred the Savoy Sultans and Erskine Hawkins, so work was irregular.
67.ch: Teddy Wilson, Cafe Society and bebop
67.q: Yes, we didn't stay too long up there with the band, because the work was very -- you know at that time they would like hire one week-end then maybe after a couple of weeks, we'd go up there for another couple days, something like that, because it wasn't regular. They didn't keep any band up there,…

409.t: The Savoy years and Charlie Buchanan
409.s: From 1955 to 1962 he led seven pieces at the Savoy, hired by manager Charlie Buchanan, who kept him because he played all the dance nights.
409.q: But the main reason why they kept me there, Helen, not because I was Cootie Williams, a jazz player. It was because I produced. They used to have certain nights for certain types of music. And I learned to play that type of music. They used to have on Wednesday nights, club nights, where they would…

379.t: The Webb-Goodman battle of music at the Savoy
379.s: He describes the packed Savoy night, Webb's pep talk, the bands' sets and big-name leaders in the crowd.
379.q: So they got so popular and so big with the Savoy Ballroom arrangement a battle of music - (unintelligible) Chick Webb and Benny Goodman. The biggest event of music has happened in the city of New York, up to moment opened that (unintelligible).

147.t: Manhattan Center ball with Dorsey and Goodman's bands
147.s: Crawford recalls Lunceford's band being unable to leave the stand at a ball packed with the top bands.
147.ch: New York, the Lafayette and the Cotton Club
147.q: Well, they were colored, Naturally, they were swingers. Whites were jitterbugging, you know, that kind of thing. I never will forget one night at Manhattan Center. I have (inaudible). We played at a ball. It was just a ball, place packed and jammed with all the biggest bands in New York City --…

120.t: Billed as Wild Bill Davison, the White Louis Armstrong, at the Savoy
120.s: At the Savoy ballroom he finds his new nickname on the canopy; the big band plays Forsythe arrangements well but falls apart without Tesh and his union card.
120.q: So, what happened was -- there was a guy who booked me in there; now, I had never been called Wild Bill Davison before - ever that I know of---

453.t: House band at Chicago's Savoy Ballroom and a failed Tulsa booking
453.s: Bernie Young's band was Savoy house band for about a year until Music Corporation of America booked it to Tulsa for a contract that fell through.
453.q: At the Savoy. No, we played -- yes, we played all the dances, we played for all the engagements that they would have there. And how we got out from there, we had booked -- how did Bernie Young get out of that contract? It took him about a whole day to get out of that, but I don't know. Music…

383.t: Battles of music: Basie, Chick Webb and Goodman at the Savoy
383.s: Wilson recalls Chick Webb's 'Get Together' beating Goodman's mixed band and speculates about a Webb-Ellington battle.
383.ch: Joining Carter and Goodman in New York
383.q: Like Basie's 'One O'Clock Jump' and Chick Webb used to play -- no band could stand up to Chick Webb when he played Get Together.1)

71.t: Band battles: Lionel Hampton, Chick Webb, Goodman, Lunceford
71.s: He recalls Basie's victories over Hampton's band, Chick Webb with Ella, and Goodman at Madison Square Garden.
71.q: Well some of the most important things that I think that I enjoyed mostly was our battle at the Savoy Ballroom. We had quite a few of them up there with all the bands. With Erskine Hawkins, Benny Goodman. But the most things that I

92.t: Paul Whiteman's poll and Eldridge's Savoy booking
92.s: Willard asks whether Whiteman's Saturday Evening Post jazz poll mattered; Collins says it brought Roy work commercially, including the Savoy.
92.ch: Paris, Lester Young, drugs, Mississippi and later sessions
92.q: Yeah, yeah. Well, he was doing -- I think they were having the jazz poll, and this was -- of all things I really believe this was a Saturday Evening Post which figures, you know, Paul Whiteman would be with the Saturday Evening Post, you know.

93.t: Why it was called sacko: the jai alai comparison
93.s: Asked about the name, Green likens sacko to jai alai with no let-up and says it competed with the Three Rhythm Kings who became Tip, Tap and Toe.
93.q: I done tacko in, but I attempted to do sacko. She would -- she got in the show -- Kate Smith, you know. Now, you can imagine what that was.

235.t: Sabby Lewis at the Savoy in Boston
235.s: Lewis was the Boston favorite with a regular spot at the Savoy; Nicholas wrote some arrangements there.
235.q: Yeah. Sabby was like the Boston favorite. They loved Sabby in Boston and he had a place called the Savoy. It was like home, you see what I mean? When we went in there we was back home and then when he went up there he knew what to play for those people up there, you see. I remember we had one…

6.t: A year and a half with Chick Webb, before the commercial turn
6.s: Procope was with Webb into 1931; the band was a local stomping jazz band at the Savoy, becoming commercial only later with Ella Fitzgerald.
6.ch: Jelly Roll's road trip, Benny Carter and Chick Webb
6.q: No, no, no, no. Chick had a good go at the Savoy Ballroom and around New York, you know, sort of -- well, it was more local, like up and down the east coast, like we'd go down to Baltimore and play a dance once in awhile or Washington and play a dance. And Atlantic City, you know,

97.t: Joining Chick Webb with Johnny Hodges in the band
97.s: Scott joins Webb's new band, and lists the members.
97.ch: Chick Webb, Lucky Roberts, Alex Jackson
97.q: because I had made money and had a little bank account. And I was more or less secure and felt more secure, and I didn't mind working.

76.t: The Savoy Ballroom: dancing, Count Basie and the bouncers
76.s: Zutty and Marge recall Ethel Waters and Louis dancing at the Savoy, taking Jimmy Dorsey there, and Count Basie asking if he would beat him to Europe. The bouncers were ex-fighters.
76.ch: Theaters, the Navy and the Singletons' partnership

171.t: Opening at the Savoy against Lucky Millinder, February 1942
171.s: Millinder's postcard threatened to send them back to the sticks; after a hard Pennsylvania drive they opened on the Sultans' bandstand.
171.ch: The McShann band on the road and at the Savoy
171.q: Oh, yeah, still is. And so, Lucky sent this telgram, we're going to send you hicks back to the sticks. Not a telegram, it was one of those one-cent postcards. And so --

473.t: Sent for by Jimmy Smith's Missourians to play the Savoy
473.s: About 1932 he was sent for to play two weeks at the Savoy with the Missourians, part of which had split off when Cab was put in front; a tape break and false start follow.
473.ch: Horace Henderson band and Roy Eldridge
473.q: He had a band, the Missourians, and it was all with Cab, and Cab -- so half of them decided to go out, because they put Cab in front of this band, and I think some of them didn't like it so well, because they was already organized. Then they were -- they was organizing their own band, so I come…

13.t: Battle of the bands with Chick Webb at the Savoy; Tuskegee
13.s: The Hines band always lost to Webb at his home ballroom.
13.ch: Joining Earl Hines and the Grand Terrace
13.q: Right. We'd lose all the time. In fact, Duke Ellington even lost. Chick Webb, boy, he had a tough band, and tough arrangements. Oh, man. Boy, he had a whole band -- our bandstand would be jumping. And we wouldn't even be playing.

79.t: Back with Henderson: the Harvest Moon Ball in Central Park
79.s: Henderson's band was reorganized in 1935. Thomas describes the free Harvest Moon Ball with Abe Lyman, crowds of 100,000 rushing the bandstand, and the move to Madison Square Garden.
79.q: I saw the damnedest thing happen I've ever seen in my life. They had a thing called the Harvest Moon Ball.
